name: Kerr Black Holes with Scalar Hair
description: A rotating black hole wrapped in a cloud of massive complex scalar field that neither falls in nor escapes, found by Carlos Herdeiro and Eugen Radu in 2014. The field turns at $m$ times the horizon's angular velocity, $\omega = m\Omega_H$, so the metric stays stationary and axisymmetric while the field changes in time and in angle. The family runs from Kerr's black holes to spinning boson stars, and its metric is known only numerically.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\lambda{}_{\mu\lambda\nu}$.
history: Two black holes in equilibrium in empty space, with the same mass and the same spin, are exactly alike, down to the quadrupole and every higher multipole of their gravitational fields [herdeiro2015review]. The uniqueness theorems that say so leave Kerr's metric as the one such black hole, and they led to the conjecture that whatever collapses, nothing is left outside but mass, spin, and charge [herdeiro2015review]. John Archibald Wheeler put the principle in the early 1970s as "Black holes have no hair" [mayo1996]. Black holes with hair of other kinds turned up through the 1990s, which, Avraham Mayo and Jacob Bekenstein wrote in 1996, "may give the impression that the principle has fallen by the wayside" [mayo1996]. "However," they went on, "this is emphatically not the case for scalar field hair" [mayo1996].¶A spinning black hole can lose some of its spin to a wave. A wave that winds round the axis more slowly than the horizon turns, $\omega < m\Omega_H$ for a frequency $\omega$, $m$ windings, and a horizon turning at $\Omega_H$, comes back from the hole stronger, carrying off some of the hole's rotational energy [herdeiro2015review]. The field's mass keeps a slow enough wave from escaping, so it scatters off the hole again and again and grows without end, the runaway that William Press and Saul Teukolsky called the black hole bomb [herdeiro2015review, press1972]. At $\omega = m\Omega_H$ exactly the wave neither grows nor dies away, and in 2012 Shahar Hod reported "stationary (infinitely long-lived) regular field configurations" around Kerr black holes spinning as fast as they can [herdeiro2015review, hod2012]. He found the height of these "clouds" above the hole in closed form [hod2012].¶Can a cloud like that keep its shape once its own weight bends the spacetime? In Aveiro, Carlos Herdeiro and Eugen Radu solved the Einstein-Klein-Gordon equations in full, for a complex field with mass, and in 2014 they found rotating black holes with the cloud built in [herdeiro2014]. The field turns in time and in angle as $e^{i(m\varphi - \omega t)}$ while its energy and momentum stay put, so the metric is stationary and axisymmetric and the field is neither [herdeiro2014]. One combination of the two symmetries leaves the field alone, the Killing vector $\partial_t + \Omega_H\,\partial_\varphi$ along which the horizon's light rays run, and the theorems that forbid hair assume the field shares all of the spacetime's symmetries [herdeiro2014, herdeiro2015review]. With $\omega = m\Omega_H$ the field turns with the horizon, and none of it flows into the hole [herdeiro2014].¶The family they found runs from Kerr's black holes, at the threshold where the clouds sit, to spinning boson stars, where the horizon shrinks to nothing [herdeiro2014]. None of them is static, since the horizon must turn at least as fast as the field of the slowest spinning boson star, and some spin faster than Kerr's bound allows, $J > GM^2/c$ [herdeiro2014, herdeiro2015construction]. Some share their mass and angular momentum with a Kerr black hole that spins fast enough for the cloud to grow on it, so two different black holes have both numbers, and of the two the hairy one has the larger horizon [herdeiro2014, herdeiro2015construction]. Each member is a numerical solution of five coupled partial differential equations on a grid, and Herdeiro and Radu mapped the family with about three thousand of them [herdeiro2015construction]. Of the five whose numbers they published in 2015, the fourth has a horizon turning at $\Omega_H = 0.82\,\mu c$, for bosons of reduced Compton wavelength $1/\mu$, and of its mass $M = 0.933\,c^2/G\mu$ the hole holds $0.234\,c^2/G\mu$ and the cloud the rest [herdeiro2015construction, herdeiro2015data].¶How heavy can such a black hole be? The heaviest have masses of about $c^2/G\mu$, which reaches the Sun's mass only for bosons lighter than about $10^{-11}$ eV, a range where no particle is known, though the string axiverse suggests some [herdeiro2014]. The cloud would show in the hole's silhouette against the sky [cunha2015]. Following light backwards from a camera past these holes in 2015, Pedro Cunha, Herdeiro, Radu, and Helgi Rúnarsson found that where the horizon and the cloud are both far from Kerr's, "novel shapes arise, sizes are considerably smaller and multiple shadows of a single BH become possible" [cunha2015]. They offered the shadows as templates for the Event Horizon Telescope [cunha2015].¶A field of spin one with a mass, a Proca field, can do the same. Proca stars came first, from Richard Brito, Vitor Cardoso, Herdeiro, and Radu, "realizing Wheeler's concept of geons for an Abelian spin 1 field" [brito2016]. Kerr black holes with Proca hair followed in 2016, from Herdeiro, Radu, and Rúnarsson [herdeiro2016proca]. On a computer, William East and Frans Pretorius let the instability run around a Kerr black hole of spin $a = 0.99\,GM/c^2$, solving the full Einstein-Proca equations [east2017]. The field took "in excess of $9\%$ of the black hole's mass", and the growth stopped by itself "when the black hole's horizon frequency decreases to match the frequency of the Proca cloud that spontaneously forms around the black hole" [east2017].

related.text: The member of the family with no field. The black holes branch off Kerr's at the threshold of superradiance, along the line of Kerr black holes that can hold a cloud of the field [herdeiro2014].

As the horizon shrinks to nothing these black holes become spinning boson stars, the turning cousins of the static stars there [herdeiro2014]. A small black hole can sit at the centre of a boson star only if the whole thing spins [herdeiro2014].

Herdeiro and Radu set their branching beside the black string's: at the onset of the Gregory-Laflamme instability a family of strings with rippled horizons branches off, as their black holes branch off Kerr's at the onset of superradiance [herdeiro2014].

Hair of another field: the black holes found beside Bartnik and McKinnon's ball of Yang-Mills field carry that field outside their horizons, against the conjecture that a black hole has no hair [volkov1999].

parameters.description: Radius of the event horizon in this chart, a length: the horizon is the sphere $r = r_H$. At $r_H = 0$ the chart is the one in which spinning boson stars are computed, with a regular centre at $r = 0$.

Dimensionless function of $r$ and $\theta$: an observer who turns at the angular velocity $cW$ has the lapse $e^{F_0}\sqrt{1 - r_H/r}$. For the black holes it is known only numerically, as a solution of the Einstein-Klein-Gordon equations that vanishes far away.

Dimensionless function of $r$ and $\theta$, the conformal factor of the plane of $r$ and $\theta$. It equals $F_2$ on the axis, which keeps the axis free of a conical singularity, and for the black holes it is known only numerically and vanishes far away.

Dimensionless function of $r$ and $\theta$: the circle of constant $t$, $r$, and $\theta$ has circumference $2\pi e^{F_2}r\sin\theta$. For the black holes it is known only numerically and vanishes far away.

Function of $r$ and $\theta$, an inverse length: $cW$ is the angular velocity at which frames are dragged round the axis. On the horizon it is constant, $cW = \Omega_H$, the angular velocity of the horizon, and the field, of frequency $\omega$ and winding number $m$ about the axis, turns with the horizon, $\omega = m\Omega_H$; far away $W$ falls as $2GJ/(c^3r^3)$ for the angular momentum $J$.

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \varphi)$ of Carlos Herdeiro and Eugen Radu, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. The four functions $F_0$, $F_1$, $F_2$, and $W$ of $r$ and $\theta$ are left free. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: Radius of the event horizon in this chart, a length: the horizon is the sphere $r = r_H$.

A positive length, the Boyer-Lindquist radius of the inner horizon, $b = -c_t$ for Herdeiro and Radu's negative constant $c_t$: the mass is $M = c^2\left(r_H + 2b\right)/2G$, the spin per unit mass is $a = \sqrt{b\left(b + r_H\right)}$, and $r = R - b$ for the Boyer-Lindquist radius $R$.

coordinates.convention: We use Herdeiro and Radu's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \varphi)$, in which the member of the family with no field is Kerr's black hole, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
